ra: Santa Muerte is the most widely venerated of the Latin American folk saints (Chesnut).
San La Muerte is a folk-canonized intercessory figure of the Litoral region (Graziano).
Maximón/San Simón is a publicly venerated Guatemalan folk saint.
Jesús Malverde is a Sinaloan folk saint (Graziano).
Niño Fidencio heads a living folk-saint devotion (fidencismo).
Sarita Colonia is a Peruvian folk saint of the marginalized (Graziano).
Difunta Correa is a major Argentine folk saint (Graziano).
San Pascualito is a Guatemalan/Chiapas folk saint of Death.
Santa Muerte's skeletal scythe-bearing iconography is a devotional reception of personified Death / the Grim Reaper (Chesnut, Devoted to Death).
San La Muerte is likewise a personification of Death received as a folk saint (Graziano).
San Pascualito is venerated as a skeletal personification of Death in Maya-Catholic devotion.
San La Muerte (Southern Cone) and Santa Muerte (Mexico) are cognate folk personifications of Death venerated as saints (Chesnut).
Maximón is publicly identified as 'San Simón,' overlaying the apostle Simon onto a Maya ancestral figure (Graziano); only the public identification is modeled.
Devotees liken Malverde's protective benefaction to a Christ-like 'generous bandit' figure; the popular name evokes Jesus, though no formal identification exists (Graziano).
Fidencista devotion publicly frames Niño Fidencio's healing ministry in imitatio Christi terms (Graziano).
Sarita Colonia's public cult casts her as a compassionate maternal intercessor for the marginalized, modeled on Marian devotion (Graziano).
The Difunta Correa devotion centers on the miraculously nursing mother, drawing on Marian maternal-intercessor imagery (Graziano).
Latin American folk sanctity adapts the Catholic cult of the saints and Marian intercession into vernacular, locally canonized figures (Graziano).
